title: CUET Political Science Test 8
subject: Political Science (Code: 323)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Political Science - 323.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: NTA CUET (UG) Political Science papers 2024 and 2026, analysed for format only (no questions copied)
textbooks: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence
instructions: Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.
One set of 5 questions is based on a passage; the set stays together.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: The UN from 1945 to 2006 in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) The WTO is set up
(B) The Human Rights Council is created
(C) The United Nations is founded
(D) The Security Council's non-permanent membership is raised from six to ten
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (C), (D), (A), (B)
Why: (C) The UN was founded in 1945. (D) The Security Council was enlarged in 1965. (A) The WTO was set up in 1995. (B) The Human Rights Council was created in 2006.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts 1965 before 1945. Option (C) puts the WTO before the Council's enlargement. Option (D) puts 2006 before 1995.
Key point: 1945 → 1965 → 1995 → 2006.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Why oil is central to world politics
questions.question: Why has oil been central to global politics?
options: A) Because only the United Nations is allowed to buy and sell it
B) Because it is found in equal amounts in every country of the world
C) Because it is used only for cooking and lighting in homes
D) Because modern economies depend on it and it brings great wealth
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Because modern economies depend on it and it brings great wealth
Why: Industrial economies depend on oil, and its control brings huge wealth and power.
Why not the others:
(A) The UN does not sell oil.
(B) Oil is concentrated in a few regions.
(C) Oil has many uses.
Key point: The politics of oil is a key part of resource geopolitics.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Basic meaning of security
questions.question: At its most basic, security means:
options: B) membership of a military alliance
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) freedom from threats
Why: In its basic sense, security means freedom from threats to core values.
Why not the others: (A), (B), (C) These are means some states use, not the meaning of security.
Key point: What counts as a threat depends on whose security we ask about.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: India and China: terms of the boundary dispute
questions.question:
Match List-I (Term) with List-II (Meaning).

List-I
(A) Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai
(B) McMahon Line
(C) Aksai Chin
(D) NEFA

List-II
(I) The area in Ladakh, in the western sector, claimed by China
(II) The earlier name of Arunachal Pradesh
(III) The boundary line in the east that China did not accept
(IV) The slogan of India–China friendship in the 1950s
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: 'Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai' was the slogan of the 1950s (IV). China did not accept the McMahon Line in the east (III). Aksai Chin is the disputed area in Ladakh (I). NEFA was the earlier name of Arunachal Pradesh (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps the slogan and the McMahon Line. Option (B) swaps the McMahon Line and Aksai Chin. Option (C) swaps Aksai Chin and NEFA.
Key point: The dispute covered both the western and the eastern sectors.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Ideology of the Soviet state
questions.question: Which ideology did the Soviet state follow?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Communism
Why: The Soviet Union was a communist state led by the Communist Party.
Why not the others: (A), (C), (D) These were not the Soviet ideology.
Key point: Communism shaped both the Soviet economy and its politics.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: The grouping India faced in 1971
questions.question: During the crisis of 1971, which grouping did India see forming against it, leading it to sign a treaty with the Soviet Union?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A US–China–Pakistan axis
Why: The USA and China drew closer and both backed Pakistan, so India signed a friendship treaty with the USSR.
Why not the others:
(A) The USSR backed India.
(B) No such bloc existed.
(D) SAARC was formed only in 1985.
Key point: Cold War alignments shaped the 1971 crisis.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: How Indira Gandhi presented the split
questions.question: How did Indira Gandhi present the conflict that led to the Congress split?
options: A) As a struggle between socialists and conservatives
B) As a quarrel between the leaders of the north and the south
C) As a dispute only over the choice of the Congress president
D) As a fight between Hindi speakers and English speakers
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) As a struggle between socialists and conservatives
Why: Indira Gandhi framed the split as an ideological struggle, which won her wide support.
Why not the others: (B), (C), (D) She did not present it in these terms.
Key point: Ideology gave her the edge over the Syndicate.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Role of the small opposition parties
questions.question: Although they won few seats in the early elections, the opposition parties played an important role because they:
options: A) criticised Congress policies and kept the government in check
B) controlled the working of the Election Commission of India
C) formed governments in most of the States after each election
D) were given a veto over all laws passed by the Parliament
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) criticised Congress policies and kept the government in check
Why: NCERT says the opposition kept up sustained criticism of the Congress and kept democracy alive.
Why not the others:
(B) The Election Commission was independent.
(C) The Congress ruled most States.
(D) No party had a veto.
Key point: A small opposition still mattered for democracy.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Country where the Kyoto Protocol was agreed
questions.question: The Kyoto Protocol takes its name from the city where it was agreed. In which country is Kyoto?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Japan
Why: Kyoto is a city in Japan.
Why not the others: (A), (C), (D) Kyoto is not in these countries.
Key point: Kyoto set binding targets for industrialised countries.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Four flows of globalisation
questions.question:
Match List-I (Flow) with List-II (Example).

List-I
(A) Ideas
(B) Capital
(C) Commodities
(D) People

List-II
(I) Investment moving from one country to another
(II) Workers migrating to other countries for jobs
(III) Goods traded across borders
(IV) Views and news spread through the media and the internet
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(II)
Why: Ideas spread through media and the internet (IV). Capital moves as investment (I). Commodities are traded goods (III). People migrate for work (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps ideas and capital. Option (B) swaps capital and commodities. Option (D) swaps commodities and people.
Key point: Globalisation is the speeding up of these flows.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: An original member of ASEAN
questions.question: Which of the following countries was a founding member of ASEAN in 1967?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Thailand
Why: Thailand was one of ASEAN's five founding members.
Why not the others: (A), (B), (D) Cambodia, Myanmar and Vietnam joined ASEAN later, in the 1990s.
Key point: ASEAN brings together ten South-East Asian states.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: India–China ties since the late 1980s
questions.question: Which statement best describes India–China relations since the late 1980s?
options: A) Trade and high-level talks have grown, though the border dispute remains.
B) The two countries have fought several border wars with each other since 1990.
C) China has joined SAARC as a full member with India's strong support.
D) India and China have agreed to merge their national currencies into one.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Trade and high-level talks have grown, though the border dispute remains.
Why: Since Rajiv Gandhi's visit in 1988, trade and talks have grown, but the boundary issue is unresolved.
Why not the others:
(B) No war has been fought since 1962.
(C) China is not a SAARC member.
(D) There is no merged currency.
Key point: Cooperation and rivalry co-exist in India–China ties.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Gorbachev's policy towards Eastern Europe
questions.question: How did Gorbachev respond when people in Eastern Europe rose against their communist governments?
options: A) He did not send Soviet forces to put down the protests.
B) He sent tanks into every country to crush the protests.
C) He asked the NATO alliance to step in and restore order.
D) He forced all these countries to join the Soviet Union.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) He did not send Soviet forces to put down the protests.
Why: Unlike earlier Soviet leaders, Gorbachev did not intervene, and the communist governments fell one after another.
Why not the others:
(B) Earlier leaders had done this, not Gorbachev.
(C) He did not ask NATO.
(D) The countries became fully independent.
Key point: Non-intervention sped the end of the Soviet bloc.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: A weakness of Japan's economy
questions.question: Which of the following is true of Japan's economy?
options: A) Japan is the largest exporter of crude oil in the whole world.
B) Japan has no major manufacturing companies of its own.
C) Japan spends most of its national income on its military.
D) It has few natural resources and imports most raw materials.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) It has few natural resources and imports most raw materials.
Why: Japan has few natural resources and imports most of its raw materials, yet it became a leading economy.
Why not the others:
(A) Japan imports oil.
(B) Japan has many famous companies.
(C) It spends about 1 per cent of GDP on its military.
Key point: Technology and industry, not resources, made Japan rich.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Shared capital of Punjab and Haryana
questions.question: Which city serves as the capital of both Punjab and Haryana?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Chandigarh
Why: Chandigarh, a Union Territory, is the capital of both States.
Why not the others:
(B), (C) Amritsar and Ludhiana are cities in Punjab.
(D) Dharamshala is a town in Himachal Pradesh.
Key point: Chandigarh's status has long been a point of dispute.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: A benefit of globalisation for consumers
questions.question: Which of the following is often cited as a benefit of globalisation for consumers?
options: A) A wider choice of goods and services
B) Fewer goods and services in the market
C) A complete ban on all imported products
D) Higher barriers to trade between countries
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A wider choice of goods and services
Why: Supporters say globalisation gives consumers more choice.
Why not the others: (B), (C), (D) These are the opposite of what globalisation brings.
Key point: Gains to consumers are weighed against costs to some workers.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Criticism of the veto
questions.question: Why is the veto power of the permanent members often criticised?
options: A) It lets the General Assembly overrule every Security Council decision.
B) It gives every single UN member an equal say in all decisions.
C) It applies only to economic and trade questions before the UN.
D) It seems undemocratic, as one member can block all the others.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) It seems undemocratic, as one member can block all the others.
Why: A single permanent member can block a decision, which many see as undemocratic.
Why not the others:
(A) The veto works within the Security Council.
(B) The veto creates inequality, not equality.
(C) It applies to substantive Security Council decisions, not only economic ones.
Key point: Reforming the veto is part of the debate on UN reform.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Former Soviet republics and their regions
questions.question:
Match List-I (Former Soviet republic) with List-II (Region).

List-I
(A) Ukraine
(B) Kazakhstan
(C) Georgia
(D) Latvia

List-II
(I) The Baltic
(II) The Caucasus
(III) Eastern Europe
(IV) Central Asia
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: Ukraine is in Eastern Europe (III). Kazakhstan is in Central Asia (IV). Georgia is in the Caucasus (II). Latvia is a Baltic state (I).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Ukraine and Kazakhstan. Option (B) swaps Kazakhstan and Georgia. Option (D) swaps Georgia and Latvia.
Key point: The fifteen republics spread across very different regions.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Name for Kashmir's shared identity
questions.question: The distinctive identity of Kashmir, shared across religious communities, is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Kashmiriyat
Why: Kashmiriyat is the name for the shared Kashmiri identity across communities.
Why not the others:
(A) Hindutva is an idea of nationhood defined by Savarkar.
(C), (D) 'Insaniyat' (humanity) and 'jamhuriyat' (democracy) are general words, not the name of this identity.
Key point: Kashmiriyat reflects the region's plural culture.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Government that appointed the Mandal Commission
questions.question: Which government appointed the Mandal Commission in 1978?
options: A) The Congress government of Indira Gandhi
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The Janata Party government
Why: The Janata Party government appointed the Second Backward Classes Commission, chaired by B.P. Mandal, in 1978.
Why not the others:
(A) Indira Gandhi's government returned only in 1980.
(B) The National Front implemented the report in 1990.
(C) The United Front came in 1996.
Key point: The report lay unimplemented for a decade.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: From devaluation to the presidential election, 1966–1969, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
(A) Fourteen banks are nationalised
(B) The rupee is devalued
(C) V.V. Giri is elected President
(D) The fourth general election is held
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B), (D), (A), (C)
Why: (B) The rupee was devalued in June 1966. (D) The fourth general election was held in February 1967. (A) The banks were nationalised in July 1969. (C) Giri was elected President in August 1969.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts the election before devaluation. Option (C) puts Giri's election before bank nationalisation. Option (D) puts bank nationalisation before the 1967 election.
Key point: June 1966 → 1967 → July 1969 → August 1969.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Name of the Syndicate's faction after the split
questions.question: After the Congress split in 1969, the faction led by the Syndicate came to be known as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) the Congress (O)
Why: The Syndicate's faction was called the Congress (O), for 'Organisation'; Indira Gandhi's was the Congress (R).
Why not the others:
(A) Congress (R) was Indira Gandhi's faction.
(B) The CFD was formed by Jagjivan Ram in 1977.
(C) Congress (I) came later.
Key point: The split was between Indira Gandhi and the old guard.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Largest contributor to the UN budget
questions.question: Which country is the largest contributor to the UN's budget?
options: D) The People's Republic of China
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The United States
Why: The USA is the largest contributor to the UN budget, which gives it great influence in the organisation.
Why not the others: (B), (C), (D) These permanent members contribute much less than the USA.
Key point: Funding gives the USA leverage over the UN.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Meaning of an arms race
questions.question: What is meant by an 'arms race'?
options: A) A treaty under which states agree to reduce their weapons
B) A UN programme to find and destroy landmines in war zones
C) A rivalry in which states keep adding weapons against each other
D) A competition among firms to sell their weapons to the UN
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A rivalry in which states keep adding weapons against each other
Why: In an arms race, each state builds weapons because its rivals do, which can make everyone less secure.
Why not the others:
(A) Reducing weapons is arms control or disarmament.
(B) This is a demining effort.
(D) The UN does not buy weapons in this way.
Key point: Arms races are a classic traditional security dilemma.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Terms from the politics of the 1990s
questions.question:
Match List-I (Term) with List-II (Meaning).

List-I
(A) Kar sevaks
(B) Hindutva
(C) Bahujan
(D) Liberalisation

List-II
(I) Removing government controls on the economy
(II) Volunteers for the construction of the Ram temple
(III) The majority made up of oppressed communities
(IV) An idea of Indian nationhood defined by V.D. Savarkar
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Why: Kar sevaks were volunteers for the temple (II). Hindutva was defined by Savarkar (IV). Bahujan means the majority of oppressed communities (III). Liberalisation removes controls (I).
Why not the others: Option (B) swaps kar sevaks and Hindutva. Option (C) swaps Hindutva and bahujan. Option (D) swaps bahujan and liberalisation.
Key point: These terms capture the 1990s debates on religion, caste and the economy.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: ASEAN, the EU and East Asia — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) ASEAN has ten members.
(B) The EU has a common foreign and defence policy that binds every member.
(C) China's growth was driven by foreign investment and foreign trade.
(D) South Korea became a member of the UN in 1991.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B) only
Why: Only (B) is false: EU members keep their own foreign and defence policies and often disagree.
Why not the others: (A) ASEAN has ten members. (C) foreign investment and trade drove China's growth. (D) South Korea joined the UN in 1991. Options (A), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: The EU integrates deeply in economics but less in foreign policy.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Climate politics — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) India's per capita carbon emissions are higher than the world average.
(B) Developed countries want all countries to share the responsibility for cutting emissions.
(C) The industrialised countries have produced most of the greenhouse gases emitted in the past.
(D) The ozone layer protects life on Earth from harmful ultraviolet rays.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A) only
Why: Only (A) is false: India's per capita emissions are far below the world average.
Why not the others: (B) the North wants responsibility to be shared. (C) the industrialised countries caused most past emissions. (D) the ozone layer blocks harmful ultraviolet rays. Options (B), (C) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: The North–South divide shapes climate negotiations.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Party founded by B.R. Ambedkar
questions.question: Which party did B.R. Ambedkar found, before he planned the Republican Party of India?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Scheduled Castes Federation
Why: Ambedkar founded the Scheduled Castes Federation and later planned the Republican Party.
Why not the others:
(A) Swatantra was founded by Rajagopalachari and others.
(B) The KMPP was founded by Acharya Kripalani.
(D) The Forward Bloc was founded by Subhas Chandra Bose.
Key point: Ambedkar was also Law Minister in Nehru's first cabinet.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: The North-East, 1963–1985, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) Manipur and Tripura become States
(B) The Assam Accord is signed
(C) Nagaland becomes a State
(D) The Mizo National Front begins an armed campaign for independence
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (D), (A), (B)
Why: (C) Nagaland became a State in 1963. (D) The MNF began its armed campaign in 1966. (A) Manipur and Tripura became States in 1972. (B) The Assam Accord was signed in 1985.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts 1966 before 1963. Option (B) puts 1972 before 1966. Option (D) puts the Accord before 1972.
Key point: 1963 → 1966 → 1972 → 1985.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: What East Pakistan became
questions.question: After Partition, the eastern wing of Pakistan was known as East Pakistan. What did it become in 1971?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Bangladesh
Why: East Pakistan became the independent country of Bangladesh in 1971.
Why not the others: (A), (B), (C) None of these was East Pakistan.
Key point: Partition's map changed again in 1971.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Head of the Janata government in 1977
questions.question: Who headed the Janata Party government formed after the 1977 election?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Morarji Desai
Why: Morarji Desai became Prime Minister at the head of the Janata government.
Why not the others:
(A) Charan Singh became Prime Minister in 1979.
(C) JP did not take office.
(D) Jagjivan Ram was not Prime Minister.
Key point: The Janata government was a coalition of rivals.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: The 1977 election and the Emergency — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Emergency showed both the weaknesses and the strengths of India's democracy.
(B) The 1977 election became a referendum on the Emergency.
(C) The Congress lost heavily in the southern States in 1977.
(D) Several opposition parties merged to form the Janata Party before the 1977 election.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: the Congress was routed in the north but did well in the southern States.
Why not the others: (A) NCERT draws lessons about democracy's weaknesses and strengths. (B) voters judged the Emergency. (D) the opposition united as the Janata Party. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: The impact of the Emergency was felt most in the north.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Number arrested under preventive detention
questions.question: About how many people were arrested under preventive detention laws during the Emergency?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1,11,000
Why: Nearly 1,11,000 people were arrested under preventive detention laws.
Why not the others: (A), (B), (C) These figures are far too low or far too high.
Key point: Mass arrests were a defining feature of the Emergency.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Politics after 1989 — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Coalition governments became the norm at the Centre after 1989.
(B) Leaders from the backward castes gained prominence in north Indian politics.
(C) The Janata Dal split into several parties in the 1990s.
(D) The BJP won a majority on its own in the 1998 election.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) coalitions ruled from 1989. (B) backward-caste leaders rose in the north. (C) the Janata Dal broke into several parties.
Why not the others: (D) is false: in 1998 the BJP won 182 seats and formed a coalition government. Options (B) and (C) include (D); option (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: The 1990s were an era of fragmented politics.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Opposition parties and their positions
questions.question:
Match List-I (Party) with List-II (Position).

List-I
(A) Swatantra Party
(B) Bharatiya Jana Sangh
(C) Socialist Party
(D) Communist Party of India

List-II
(I) Inspired by the Russian revolution, it worked for a communist society
(II) Wanted Hindi to replace English as the official language
(III) Favoured a free economy and opposed land ceilings
(IV) Criticised the Congress for favouring capitalists and landlords
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(II), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Why: The Swatantra Party favoured a free economy and opposed land ceilings (III). The Jana Sangh wanted Hindi as the official language (II). The Socialists accused the Congress of favouring capitalists and landlords (IV). The CPI drew inspiration from the Russian revolution (I).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Swatantra and the Jana Sangh. Option (B) swaps the Jana Sangh and the Socialists. Option (C) swaps the Socialists and the CPI.
Key point: The opposition ranged from the free-market right to the communist left.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: What made the 2014 result stand out
questions.question: What made the result of the 2014 Lok Sabha election stand out?
options: A) The Congress won its largest-ever majority.
B) No party won more than 100 seats.
C) For the first time since 1984, a single party won a majority on its own.
D) Regional parties formed the government without national parties.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) For the first time since 1984, a single party won a majority on its own.
Why: In 2014 the BJP won a majority on its own, which no party had done since the Congress in 1984.
Why not the others:
(A) The Congress won only 44 seats.
(B) The BJP won 282 seats.
(D) A national party formed the government.
Key point: 2014 broke a 30-year pattern of hung or coalition verdicts.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: Why tribal people opposed mining and steel projects in Odisha
questions.question: Why did tribal people oppose the plans for iron-ore mining and steel plants in Odisha?
options: A) They wanted the steel plants to be built in other countries instead.
B) They feared displacement and the loss of their land and livelihood.
C) They wanted the State to import all of the steel it would need.
D) They opposed every kind of modern industry on religious grounds.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) They feared displacement and the loss of their land and livelihood.
Why: Tribal people feared they would be displaced and lose their land and livelihoods; environmentalists also worried about pollution.
Why not the others:
(A) They were not asking for plants abroad.
(C) Imports were not their demand.
(D) Their concerns were about land and livelihood.
Key point: Development raises hard questions about who gains and who loses.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Kinds of human rights
questions.question:
Match List-I (Idea) with List-II (Example or meaning).

List-I
(A) Political rights
(B) Economic rights
(C) Rights of minorities and indigenous peoples
(D) Humanitarian intervention

List-II
(I) Freedom of speech and assembly
(II) Action by outside powers to stop mass abuses in a country
(III) The right to work, food and a basic livelihood
(IV) The right to a cultural identity of one's own
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: Political rights include free speech and assembly (I). Economic rights include work and food (III). Minorities and indigenous peoples claim cultural identity (IV). Humanitarian intervention means outside action to stop abuses (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps political and economic rights. Option (C) swaps economic and minority rights. Option (D) swaps minority rights and humanitarian intervention.
Key point: Human rights debates raise hard questions about sovereignty.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: Basis of India's nuclear doctrine
questions.question: India's nuclear doctrine is based on the idea of:
options: B) first use of nuclear weapons in any war
C) giving up all nuclear weapons at once
D) sharing nuclear weapons with its allies
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) credible minimum nuclear deterrence
Why: India's doctrine rests on credible minimum deterrence, along with no first use.
Why not the others:
(B) India has a no-first-use policy.
(C) India has not given up its weapons.
(D) India does not share weapons.
Key point: India sees its weapons as a deterrent, not for aggression.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Gandhi, Partition and integration — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) On 15 August 1947 Gandhi was not in Delhi but in Kolkata, working to stop communal riots.
(B) Gandhi was assassinated on 30 January 1948 by Nathuram Godse.
(C) After Gandhi's assassination, the RSS was banned for some time.
(D) Hyderabad joined India by signing the Instrument of Accession in August 1947.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) Gandhi spent Independence Day in Kolkata. (B) Godse shot him on 30 January 1948. (C) the government banned the RSS for a while.
Why not the others: (D) is false: the Nizam refused to join, and Hyderabad was integrated only after a military operation in September 1948. Options (C) and (D) include (D); option (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Gandhi's death shocked the nation into acting against communal hatred.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: Plans and programmes, 1951–1970, in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
(A) The Second Five Year Plan begins
(B) The First Five Year Plan begins
(C) Operation Flood begins
(D) Planning is suspended in a 'plan holiday'
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (B), (A), (D), (C)
Why: (B) The First Plan began in 1951. (A) The Second Plan began in 1956. (D) The plan holiday began in 1966. (C) Operation Flood began in 1970.
Why not the others: Option (B) puts the Second Plan before the First. Option (C) puts the plan holiday before the Second Plan. Option (D) puts Operation Flood before the plan holiday.
Key point: 1951 → 1956 → 1966 → 1970.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: Why the leaders accepted linguistic States
questions.question: Why did the national leadership finally accept the reorganisation of States on linguistic lines?
options: A) Because the British had made a binding promise of it before leaving
B) Because the Supreme Court had ordered the government to do it
C) Because popular movements showed it would strengthen national unity
D) Because Pakistan had already created its own linguistic provinces
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Because popular movements showed it would strengthen national unity
Why: Movements like the one in Andhra convinced leaders that recognising languages would make the nation more democratic and united.
Why not the others:
(A) The British made no such promise binding on India.
(B) No court ordered it.
(D) Pakistan's choices did not decide India's policy.
Key point: Linguistic States accepted diversity within unity.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Congress tally in the 1989 election
questions.question: How many Lok Sabha seats did the Congress win in the 1989 election, when it lost power but remained the largest party?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 197
Why: The Congress won 197 seats in 1989, far fewer than in 1984, and the National Front formed the government.
Why not the others:
(A) 415 was its tally in 1984.
(C) 145 was its tally in 2004.
(D) 352 was the Congress (R)'s tally in 1971.
Key point: 1989 ended the Congress's dominance.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Year communist governments fell across Eastern Europe
questions.question: In which year did the communist governments of Eastern Europe fall one after another?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1989
Why: In 1989 communist governments across Eastern Europe collapsed in quick succession.
Why not the others:
(A) 1968 saw the Prague Spring crushed.
(B) 1979 saw the invasion of Afghanistan.
(C) 1985 is when Gorbachev came to power.
Key point: 1989 ended the Soviet bloc in Eastern Europe.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: The work of international organisations — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The IMF oversees financial institutions and regulations that act at the international level.
(B) The World Bank gives loans and grants to member countries.
(C) In the WTO, decisions are taken unanimously, but the major economic powers have used it to frame rules in their interest.
(D) Amnesty International is an agency of the United Nations.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) the IMF oversees international finance. (B) the World Bank gives loans and grants. (C) the major powers have shaped WTO rules despite unanimity.
Why not the others: (D) is false: Amnesty International is an NGO, not a UN agency. Options (B) and (D) include (D); option (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Inter-governmental bodies and NGOs both shape world politics.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Majority community in Sri Lanka
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Sri Lanka has kept a democratic political system since it became independent in 1948, but it has faced a long and bitter ethnic conflict. Its politics came to be dominated by forces representing the Sinhala majority, and some argued that the island should belong to the Sinhalas alone. Tamils, both those long settled in the north and east and those whose families had come from India as plantation workers, felt neglected, and Tamil nationalism turned militant. From 1983 the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam waged an armed struggle for a separate Tamil state in the north and east. Tamils in India pressed the Indian government to act. In 1987 India signed an accord with Sri Lanka and sent a peacekeeping force, but the force was drawn into fighting with the militants and withdrew in 1989 without achieving its aim. Later, Norway and Iceland tried to bring the two sides to the negotiating table. Despite the conflict, Sri Lanka recorded considerable economic growth and high levels of human development. It was among the first developing countries to control the growth of its population and the first country in South Asia to liberalise its economy. The armed conflict ended in 2009 with the defeat of the militants.

Question: According to the passage, Sri Lankan politics came to be dominated by forces representing which community?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The Sinhalas
Why: The passage says politics came to be dominated by forces representing the Sinhala majority.
Why not the others:
(A) The Tamils felt neglected.
(C) Muslims are not mentioned.
(D) Plantation workers were among the Tamils who felt neglected.
Key point: Majority dominance fed minority resentment.

Question: From which year, according to the passage, did the militants wage an armed struggle for a separate Tamil state?

Why: The passage says the armed struggle began in 1983.
Why not the others:

Question: What does the passage say about the peacekeeping force India sent in 1987?
options: A) It got drawn into fighting and withdrew in 1989, its aim unmet.
B) It defeated the militants within a year and brought the conflict to an end.
C) It was sent at the militants' own request to protect the Tamil areas.
D) It stayed on in Sri Lanka until the armed conflict ended in 2009.

Question: Read the four claims below. Which one goes against what the passage says about Sri Lanka?
options: A) Sri Lanka was the first South Asian country to liberalise its economy.
B) Sri Lanka was among the first developing countries to control population growth.
C) The conflict wrecked Sri Lanka's economy and kept its human development low.
D) Sri Lanka has had a democratic system since independence.

Why: The passage says that despite the conflict Sri Lanka recorded considerable growth and high human development.
Why not the others: (A), (B), (D) The passage states each of these.

questions.question:

Question: What can best be inferred from the mention of Norway and Iceland in the passage?
options: A) They sent their own troops to fight the militants after India withdrew.
B) Countries besides India also tried to end the conflict through talks.
C) They wanted Sri Lanka to apply for membership of the European Union.
D) They openly supported the creation of a separate Tamil state in the north.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Countries besides India also tried to end the conflict through talks.
Why: The passage says Norway and Iceland tried to bring the two sides to the negotiating table, which shows outside mediation beyond India.
Why not the others:
(A) No troops are mentioned.
(C) The EU is not mentioned.
(D) They acted as mediators, not as supporters of either side.
